claims.text: Nanostructured ZrB2 powder will be consolidated by SPS under a reducing atmosphere at 1800–2000 °C.
SPS at 1800–2000 °C will produce single-phase ZrB2.
The SPS product will be fully dense and have minimal porosity.
SPS will lower the required ZrB2 preparation temperature from above 2300 °C to 1800–2000 °C.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will resist liquid-plating-bath-induced defects better than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C.
Conventionally prepared ZrB2 typically has larger grains, higher porosity, and more defects than the proposed SPS material.
Defects in conventional ZrB2 act as liquid-ingress pathways during plating.
Pulsed DC current and rapid SPS heating will minimize grain growth.
Localized Joule heating and rapid thermal cycles enhance diffusion kinetics and permit densification at lower temperatures.
Nanostructured starting powders restrict grain growth and pore coalescence.
Reduced pore coalescence minimizes channels for liquid infiltration during plating-bath exposure.
The SPS-processed ZrB2 will have improved mechanical strength.
The SPS-processed ZrB2 will form fewer holes or defects during prolonged liquid plating bath exposure.
Maintaining a uniform nanostructure and full densification may become more variable in larger samples.
A controlled comparison will use conventionally sintered ZrB2 prepared above 2300 °C and SPS ZrB2 prepared at 1800–2000 °C under a reducing atmosphere.
Both sample sets will undergo identical extended plating-bath exposure and be compared for density, porosity, grain size, mechanical strength, and hole or defect formation.
The hypothesis will be falsified if the SPS samples do not show significantly lower porosity, improved strength, and reduced hole or defect formation relative to conventional samples.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis, intervention, and experiment require a reducing atmosphere, while the conditions permit either an inert or reducing atmosphere and give argon or vacuum as examples. These are not equivalent atmospheric requirements.
